name: expectation confirmed
description: Moderate positivity coming from a perception that an important expectation was confirmed. It's a brief mild happiness about being correct, separate from the implications of being right.
perceptions: To survive in the world, I need to understand it.
A perception matching my expectation proves that I understand this part of the world correctly.
I had prepared myself for a particular outcome that seemed to be important.
results: Confirming an expectation is just the first spark of what may be an avalanche of sensations. If you were right about expecting something good, you'll be happy. If you were right about something bad, you'll still be sad, but you may feel some consolation in having correctly expected the bad thing.
examples: Correctly expecting your uncle would be late to dinner.
The election went the way you expected.

guidance.description: Being right feels nice. So nice that your brain can actually bend perception through several different cognitive biases. This is why scientists try to be careful before celebrating. Most people much happier when they feel they can trust their intuitions about being right, but for really important things you might consider at least being aware of common biases.

variations.name: prediction confirmed
variations.description: A twinge of positivity coming from a perception that a low-impact prediction was found to be correct. It's a brief mild happiness about being correct, separate from the implications of being right.
perceptions: In order to live in the world, I need to understand it.
This perception confirming my prediction suggests that I understand this part correctly.
It's a good I was right, but it doesn't affect me all that much.
results: A prediction succeeding is the first spark of what may be many sensations. If you were right about predicting something good, you may be doubly satisfied. If you were right about a prediction of something bad happening, you'll still have to deal with the bad thing, but have the consolation of having predicted correctly.
examples: Finishing the Wordle after thinking you would solve it.
The sports team won as predicted.

variations.name: guess confirmed
variations.description: A mild satisfaction coming from a perception that a low-impact prediction was found to be correct.
perceptions: In order to live in the world, I need to understand it.
This perception confirming my guess suggests that I understand this part correctly.
results: A correct guess is perceived as no big deal.
examples: You correctly estimated the number of beans in a jar.

comparisons.description: These are all similar, differing in how much confidence you had in the pattern and the impact to your life. You're most invested in 'core assumptions' and 'expectations', so finding one that's right gives you a little satisfaction even if the outcome turns out to be negative. You're not very invested in 'predictions' so a 'prediction confirmation' doesn't matter so much in the big picture. Finally, you're not emotionally invested in a 'guess' at all, so after a tiny rush of satisfaction about being right, you've already moved on.

Being wrong about something generally creates more negativity than being right creates positivity. The brain's reward system is asymmetric: it rewards us a little for being right, but can punish us sternly for being wrong.

commentaries.quote: A correct answer is like an affectionate kiss.

Trying to be less wrong is better than trying to be right. When you focus on being less wrong, blindspots become visible, beliefs no longer need protecting, and you become open to better ideas. Outcome over ego.
Confidence comes not from always being right but from not fearing to be wrong.
There is more to knowing than just being correct.
People who care more about being right than ending right prove just how wrong they were all along.
